Traditions connect generations, carrying the cultural and moral values of ancestors to new generations, giving them a sense of identity and belonging. Some of these traditions are so lovely that they are adopted more widely. The beautiful old Christmas tradition of Christmas wheat is one of them.

The sowing of Christmas wheat is a tradition across Europe from France to Ukraine and the Balkans. Early in December, people “plant” wheatgrass seeds in bowls indoors early in December and let the shoots grow until Christmas. Initially the growing wheat seeds were considered a blessing for the coming harvest. But beyond that, the green shoots have come to symbolize fertility, new life, and eternal renewal.

You don’t have to live in the South of France or other parts of Europe to practice this lovely tradition. We’ll tell you all about the custom of growing wheatgrass indoors and how you can make it your own this Christmas.

All around the globe, cultural heritage shapes how people celebrate, and also how they express beauty. The lovely tradition of planting Christmas wheat is still very much a part of Christmas festivities in Europe, thought to have been inherited from the Romans.

It is practiced in the Province area of France, as well as Croatia, Ukraine, and parts of Italy and Portugal, each region claiming it as their own. In Province, it is called Saint-Barbe wheat (le blé de la Sainte-Barbe) because the day of planting, December 4, is the feast day of Saint Barbara. By Christmas day, the seeds have grown fresh green shoots that become decorations on the Christmas table.

In Province, this age-old tradition involves sprouting grains of wheat in three separate bowls. The ritual is said to ensure prosperity and happiness for the coming year, a promise memorialized in the old Provençal adage, “when wheat goes well, everything goes well.”

In Croatia, the origins of this tradition are still related to religion, but they are different. Growing wheatgrass is related to the story of the holy family fleeing Herod’s soldiers. It is said that the family found a farmer sowing wheat. The family requested that the farmer tell the Herod’s soldiers that the family had already passed through.

The wheat grew remarkably fast that year so by the time the soldiers came, there was a fine crop. Then, the farmer told them that the family passed through while he was sowing his crop. Because the wheat was so tall, the soldiers assumed that the family had passed by long ago and abandoned their quest. As such, wheat seeds are sown in December to represent light found amid the winter's darkness.

Well, if you would like to incorporate this ancient tradition into your own holiday celebrations, we’ll walk you through the steps. There are three: gather what you need, “plant” the seeds, then arrange the centerpiece.

The most important "ingredient" you will require to grow your own Christmas wheat are the wheat grains themselves. Traditionally, you use hard red winter wheat berries (sold as "wheatgrass seeds”) although it is possible to use alternatives like lentils or chickpeas instead.

The presentation also varies from region to region. In Province, for Saint Barbe’s wheat, they use three small bowls or saucers and damp cotton wool. The three containers have religious significance, representing the Holy Trinity. In Croatia, you can use any container, but you still need to line it with either cotton wool or soil as a growing medium. A more practical alternative is to use a growing tray filled with potting soil with a solid tray beneath it to catch water.

Soak the grains overnight in water. After that, place them evenly on the growing medium - like the bed of damp cotton wool or the potting soil. If you are using three bowls, spread it evenly between them. If you are using a tray, spread the seeds there.

Place the seeded container near a bright window at a mild temperature. Spray it with water and cover with plastic paper or a plastic bag. Remove this plastic when the seeds begin to germinate.

Mist the cotton with water daily to keep it moist. This allows the shoots to germinate and grow straight and green.

How you choose to arrange the centerpiece depends entirely on your own preferences and traditions. By Christmas Eve, the little shoots are green and straight,

In Croatia, the wheat sprouts are often decorated with the Croatian tricolour – a red-white-blue ribbon. This adds patriotic symbolism. The Croatians sometimes add a red candle or even a red apple in the centre of the container to add more holiday cheer.

In Province, the French often toe up the sprouted wheat with red and yellow or red and green ribbons. The wheat display becomes the centerpiece for their traditional Christmas Eve feast. After Christmas, the French place the pots in or near the family crèche (aka the nativity scene) alongside handmade clay saint images. Finally, the wheat can be planted in open ground or burned in the fireplace for protection.

Remember, this is a lovely tradition, but while wheatgrass might look like a microgreen it should not be used as one. Yes, it has many incredible health properties (it is said to prevent some types of cancer, fight infection and improve cognitive function), but it is not edible.

That being said, you can juice it and drink its juice, which is full of vitamins, minerals, and antioxidants. Sounds like a great tipple after a big holiday feast, eh?

Teo Spengler is a master gardener and a docent at the San Francisco Botanical Garden, where she hosts public tours. She has studied horticulture and written about nature, trees, plants and gardening for more than two decades. Before turning her focus to gardening, she worked as an attorney and legal writer, experience she also brings to her role as our Gardening Lawyer. Her extended family includes some 30 houseplants and hundreds of outdoor plants, including 250 trees, which are her main passion. Spengler currently splits her life between San Francisco and the French Basque Country, though she was raised in Alaska, giving her experience of gardening in a range of climates.

#7829. Social Media Platforms Not Liable for Racist Buffalo Mass Shooting, Says N.Y. High Court by 4-3 Vote

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

But a majority of the judges seem to endorse liability for "addictive design" in other cases (which wouldn't involve liability for spreading particular viewpoints).

From the 4-judge unsigned majority opinion in Patterson v. Meta Platforms, Inc., decided today by N.Y.'s high court:

On May 14, 2022, a man motivated by heinous white supremacist ideologies he allegedly adopted due to content he viewed on social media carried out a mass shooting at a Buffalo grocery store, killing 10 and injuring three others. Plaintiffs, victims of the shooting and their family members, commenced these actions against the shooter's parents, firearms manufacturers, and social media companies, seeking compensation for their injuries.

These appeals concern motions to dismiss plaintiffs' claims against several social media companies whose platforms the shooter allegedly used before committing this unspeakable act of violence. Specifically, plaintiffs contend that their complaints state causes of action for products liability based on defective features of these social media defendants' platforms and their failure to warn thereof….

[P]laintiffs failed to adequately plead that features of [the] social media defendants' products proximately caused their injuries. Generally, a defendant's acts qualify as a proximate cause when they are "a substantial cause of the events which produced the injury." This inquiry examines

"the foreseeability of the event resulting in injury; the passage of time between the originally negligent act and the intervening act; the spatial gap, if any, between the original act and the intervening act; whether the original act of negligence was a completed occurrence or was ongoing at the time of the intervening act; whether and, if so, what other forces combined to bring about the harm; as well as public policy considerations regarding the scope of liability."

Foreseeability is often the most significant factor. Indeed, if an unforeseeable intervening criminal act of a third party causes the plaintiff's injury, the causal connection is severed. Thus, proximate causation will not be found when the intervening act "is extraordinary under the circumstances, not foreseeable in the normal course of events, or independent of or far removed from the defendant's conduct." "Although foreseeability and proximate cause are generally questions for the factfinder, there are instances in which proximate cause can be determined as a matter of law because 'only one conclusion may be drawn from the established facts'" such as when "the original negligent act merely 'furnished the occasion for'—but did not cause—'an unrelated act to cause injuries not ordinarily anticipated.'"

Here, plaintiffs failed to adequately allege that the remaining social media defendants' product defects proximately caused the shooter to carry out the mass shooting that resulted in plaintiffs' injuries. The complaints, even accepting the factual allegations as true, fail to establish that the shooter's actions were a natural and foreseeable consequence of these defendants' decisions about how to design and operate their platforms.

Instead, under the circumstances, the shooter's actions were so extraordinary as to sever the causal chain as a matter of law. {Our conclusion is limited to the unusual facts of this case, where the platforms' assertedly addictive features were alleged to have harmed the shooter rather than the plaintiffs directly.} We therefore need not address the scope of section 230 of the Communications Decency Act or how it would apply to the claims against these defendants.

Judge Halligan joined the majority, but also wrote a concurring opinion:

I join the majority because I agree that the plaintiffs have not adequately pleaded proximate causation. I write separately to underscore that, for me, this conclusion rests squarely on the highly unusual facts presented here, and to offer some additional thoughts regarding the scope of section 230.

As an initial matter, I agree with my dissenting colleagues that the plaintiffs alleged that several of the defendants tortiously designed addictive products. The complaints make a number of general claims about social media and youth: that defendants' platforms are addictive; that compulsive use of social media, particularly by young people, causes emotional disturbance and "impulsive decision-making and risk-taking behavior"; and that such use can also yield other deleterious consequences, including "sleep disturbances, mental health problems and suicidal ideation, and violent, hateful acts." The complaints further assert that the social media defendants, knowing of the addictive quality of their products and the heightened susceptibility of young users, not only failed to implement features for limiting use or warning parents, but also took deliberate advantage of that vulnerability by utilizing "strategic timing and clustering of notifications to lure back users" and by implementing "barriers to the deactivation and deletion of accounts." …

I find the claims before us quite distinct from the cases cited by the dissent that have allowed products liability claims premised on the addictiveness of social media platforms to proceed. I have little doubt that a plaintiff could allege a sufficient connection between the design of a platform and adverse consequences for the mental health of young users. In those cases, the harms that form the basis for the claims—for example, the alleged inducement of "compulsive use among young users to the detriment of their health and well-being"—flow directly from the platforms' allegedly defective features, leaving little question "that the defective design was a substantial factor in causing plaintiff's injury."

But the plaintiffs here are not bringing a claim on behalf of users. Instead, they are seeking recompense for the victims of a crime committed by a social media user. In other words, the allegedly addictive properties of the platforms were not alleged to have harmed the plaintiffs here directly, but rather to have harmed the shooter, who in turn engaged in extensive research and planning before murdering ten people and wounding others…. I do not see the connection between the two as sufficiently articulated to allow the case to proceed.

Three aspects of these claims inform my conclusion. First, although intervening criminal acts do not necessarily sever the causal chain, the shooter's conduct was apparently painstakingly planned and extraordinarily violent.

Second, the prominence of content in many of plaintiffs' allegations gives me real pause. Even if we were to interpret section 230 as not immunizing defendants against claims for actions that rest, at least in part, on content, I am not aware of other instances where a court has held that provocative content proximately caused someone to commit a violent crime, and I am hesitant to take that step here. {I understand the plaintiffs to disclaim on appeal any effort to base liability on defendants' roles as publishers of content. But their complaints can be read to allege that the platforms are defective at least in part because of the racist and extremist content they make available, and the plaintiffs acknowledge that content is a necessary link in the causal chain leading to their harms.}

Third, the defendants' platforms have billions of worldwide users. To the extent that proximate cause could rest on a correlation between social media use and a specific type of harmful act committed by any one of those users, the potential liability would sweep broadly, to say the least. If all such conduct were "a natural and foreseeable consequence" of a platform's design choices, the concept of proximate cause would have little meaning….

As for section 230, …. "we [have] read section 230 to bar 'lawsuits seeking to hold a service provider liable for its exercise of a publisher's traditional editorial functions.'" … Our endorsement of a "traditional editorial functions" test for section 230 immunity, however, does little to answer whether the conduct of modern social media platforms can be labelled such a function.

As to claims that a defendant designed its platform features to encourage or facilitate addiction, irrespective of the particular content promoted by the platform, I agree with the dissent that they are not barred by section 230. That is because such conduct does not constitute a traditional editorial function, even under a broad understanding of that term.

As to claims that challenge a social media platform's use of content-recommendation algorithms, the dissent appears to take the view that content-recommendation algorithms which are designed to be addictive are not covered by section 230 immunity, since they increase engagement in a way that could not have been envisioned at the time that provision was enacted in 1996. I have no quarrel with how we framed the scope of section 230 in Shiamili: the key question is whether a platform engaged in a traditional editorial function, akin to a decision "to publish, withdraw, postpone or alter content." But whether platforms' use of content-recommendation algorithms can be said to resemble traditional decisions to publish, withdraw, postpone, or alter content is, for me, a more difficult question….

[O]verly broad interpretations of section 230 in the face of a rapidly changing technological landscape are unmoored from Congress's purpose in enacting that provision—to protect minors from being exposed to pornography online…. Given that caution, I would not be inclined to extend section 230's reach to all content-recommendation algorithms. I am particularly skeptical that use of individualized content-recommendation algorithms—that is, algorithms that "assess[ ] a user's prior posts, friends, or viewing habits to recommend new content and connections"—constitutes a traditional publisher function. After all, "[t]raditional publication has never included selecting the news, opinion pieces, or classified ads to send to each individual reader based on guesses as to their preferences and interests." Instead, such functions may be "more analogous to the actions of a direct marketer, matchmaker, or recruiter than to those of a publisher."

In my view, a closer question is presented as to engagement-maximizing algorithms that, unlike the algorithms described above, do not take into account any individual user's conduct but instead seek to "promote[ ] third-party content" based on "cumulative user engagement." On one hand, algorithms that do not respond to individual user conduct may be thought to resemble a publisher's traditional aim of presenting content that users, on the whole, want to see. On the other hand, one might conclude that "generic" content-based algorithms bear no more resemblance to traditional publication than their "'advanced'—individualized—counterparts" because they still rely on an assessment of user viewing habits in a manner akin to "a direct marketer" rather than a traditional publisher. My dissenting colleagues offer yet another variation on this point; they assert that engagement-maximizing algorithms differ from an editor's choice of where to place a news story because the algorithms are "designed to prey on neurological frailties and alter brain chemistry."

Whether section 230 protects any of these algorithms is, for me, a difficult question, and I do not think the record before us sheds much light on how different types of content-recommendation algorithms actually operate on the social media defendants' individual platforms—information that might affect my view. We need not decide those questions today because, whatever the scope of the "traditional editorial functions" protected by section 230, the plaintiffs have failed to sufficiently allege that the defendants' platforms' features caused their grave injuries.

Judge Rivera, joined by Chief Judge Wilson and Judge Troutman, dissented in relevant part; an excerpt from the very long opinion:

The complaints detail the shooter's transformation from a seemingly ordinary teenager into a virulent racist and violent white supremacist…. [In his manifesto, t]he shooter also wrote that he "was not born racist nor [did he] gr[o]w up to be racist." Rather, he was exposed to and indoctrinated in his ideology of racial violence after using various social media platforms, starting with Instagram, YouTube, and Snapchat in his early teen years, before he transitioned to more niche platforms like Reddit, Discord, Twitch and 4chan. The shooter claimed he quickly "became transfixed with and addicted to [the] online world." He wrote in his diary:

"I'm addict[ed] to consoooooming. It's 2 in the morning. w[hat] t[he] f[*ck] … I'll admit my mental health has seriously degraded these past few years, especially in the last few months. I should be sleeping right now. I'm just browsing online:/" (emphasis added).

By his own account, he sacrificed "years of [his] life" to being online, often "stay[ing] up late" "browsing Reddit or watching YouTube" "every day." He stated that his compulsive social media use "seriously degraded" his mental health and isolated him from his peers. Rather than "go[ing] to friend's houses" or other social gatherings, "[e]very day after school [he] would just go home and play games and watch YouTube, mostly by [him]self." Ultimately, as he descended further into isolation, he believed he had no other choice but to commit this barbarous act.

Plaintiffs allege that the shooter's experience of compulsive social media engagement is widespread because the products' addictive features are fundamental to the social media defendants' business model. According to plaintiffs, defendants' business models seek to maximize user engagement through products "designed to be addictive." Plaintiffs assert that the operation of these products on the shooter, and their adverse impact on his mind caused by their addictive features, are links in the proximate causal chain underlying plaintiffs' tort liability causes of action against the social media defendants….

The Appellate Division erroneously concluded that defendants are immune from plaintiffs' lawsuit under Section 230. As I discuss, Section 230 does not shield defendants from plaintiffs' products liability and failure to warn allegations grounded on allegedly addictive products, as those claims have nothing to do with defendants' role as a third-party content publisher or as the creator of protected speech….

To the extent plaintiffs' claims against the social media defendants are based upon defendants' publication of third-party content, including racist, white supremacist, and violent content, defendants are immune from suit pursuant to Section 230. However, not all claims asserted in the complaints are based upon defendants' publication of third-party content. Rather, as I explain, the complaints also stated causes of action based on defendants' design of allegedly defective products and failure to warn….

Plaintiffs assert that these defendants are civilly liable for their role in addicting the shooter to social media and consequent deterioration of his mental health. Plaintiffs' complaints set forth the entire chain of causation that allegedly led to the mass shooting. By designing highly addictive algorithms known to cause severe mental harm to teenagers—like the shooter—the social media defendants created a direct link to the resulting damages, particularly given their failure to warn users and parents of these risks…. [T]here is no Section 230 immunity that attaches to the architecture of defendants' social media products—particularly their purposefully addictive algorithms….

Defendants' alternative argument that the complaints were properly dismissed on First Amendment grounds is unpersuasive. At this pre-answer stage of the litigation, it is unclear how precisely the content-recommendation algorithms function, meaning it is not possible to determine, as a matter of law, on a motion to dismiss that the algorithms themselves are protected speech. That determination requires factual findings dependent on future discovery. On a motion to dismiss we only decide whether the plaintiffs' claim is cognizable and not whether it will eventually succeed based on the facts established by the record….

And here's a short excerpt from the dissent's long discussion of why it rejects the majority's proximate cause theory:

The majority's conclusion that plaintiffs "fail to establish that the shooter's actions were a natural and foreseeable consequence" of the social media defendants' platforms because "the shooter's actions were so extraordinary as to sever the causal chain as a matter of law" is unsupported by our well-established tort liability doctrines. First, we have made clear that there may be more than one link in a causal chain and there may be more than one tortfeasor liable, jointly or individually, for a plaintiff's injuries. "[T]he mere fact that other persons share some responsibility for [the] plaintiff's harm does not absolve [a] defendant from liability." Thus, the fact that the third-party content creators may bear responsibility for the harm does not mean that defendants bear none.

Second, a defect need only be a "substantial cause"—not the sole cause—"of the events which produced the injury." Substantial means more than slight or trivial. Plaintiffs' allegations that defendants' product adversely affected the shooter's mental health and behavior, making him a compulsive social media user, with the attendant negative impact on his mind and body, isolated from others, rendering him more susceptible to commit this horrific violent act, easily satisfies the "substantial cause" standard.

Third, not all intervening acts break the causal chain. An intervening act only breaks the causal nexus if it is extraordinary under the circumstances, unforeseeable in the normal course of events, or independent of and far removed from the defendant's conduct. That determination depends on whether the intervening act and its consequences were the foreseeable result of a defendant's tortious conduct. Even the "intentional" or "criminal" intervening acts of a third party can be reasonably foreseeable….

[W]hile here, the harm arose from exposure to graphic violence and white supremacist propaganda, plaintiffs allege that the algorithm is content-agnostic. According to plaintiffs, defendants' products and platforms rely on these complex algorithms to keep users engaged, which negatively impacts young people's mental health, and, in turn, increases the tendency to violent behavior, all the while driving revenue for these defendants. Thus, the majority's assertion that the shooter's actions were not foreseeable is nothing more than a factual conclusion, but that determination cannot be made by the Court on a motion to dismiss….

Eric A. Shumsky, Moez M. Kaba, and Lisa LeCours are listed as representing the platforms.

#7828. Shrubs Steal the Show in Bonnie’s Colorado Garden

Hi GPOD! Yesterday we enjoyed some beautiful fall color in Nancy’s Massachusetts garden, and today we’re heading west to see what fall looked like in Colorado this year.

Bonnie took these photos in mid-November after an unusually long fall. While the trees certainly put on a show, Bonnie says the shrubs were the real stars this year. Here’s Bonnie:

Colorado put on a spectacular fall color display this year. My garden was filled with so many vivid hues that I had to capture them in photos. Some years are more colorful than others, and this was certainly a good one! The standout colors came not from the trees, but from the shrubs.

Welcome to my fall garden! Just walk through the arch and see the colors beyond. ‘Forest Pansy’ eastern redbud (Cercis canadensis ‘Forest Pansy’, Zones 5–9) starts in spring with dark burgundy leaves, turns green by late summer, and finishes the season in bright yellow. I love this tree!

Other stars in my fall garden are the barberries, hydrangeas, dwarf smokebushes (Cotinus coggygria cvs., Zones 4–8), and spireas. Oh, and the Diabolo ninebark (Physocarpus opulifolius ‘Monlo’, Zones 3–7) in the back turned a lovely red this year.

Barberry, dwarf smokebush, and spireas in the back make a nice composition.

I’m in love with these ‘Annabelle’ smooth hydrangeas (Hydrangea arborescens ‘Annabelle’, Zones 3–9). They are all over my yard.

Another hydrangea vignette with viburnum, boxwood, and Japanese forest grass (Hakonechloa macra, Zones 5–9) in front.

I love the beautiful colors of this barberry.

Around the other side of our yard, the dwarf smokebush shines among the evergreens and the orange leaves of the mountain ash and honey locust (Gleditsia triacanthos, Zones 3–8) trees.

Looking toward the front yard, the dwarf smokebush steals the show!

A weeping Norway spruce (Picea abies, Zones 3–7) and barberry make a beautiful combination.

Thanks for sharing your beautiful fall garden with us, Bonnie! The trees are gorgeous, but I agree that the shrubs really stole the show this year.

Before you could buy suet cakes, birders stirred up treats from the pantry. Marvel Meal is one of the good ones, and you don't even have to turn on the stove.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Go down the bird food aisle this time of year and the choices just keep going, from seed blends to suet cakes in a dozen flavors. Some people walk right past all of it. They make their own at home, and one old recipe shows up in their kitchens again and again.

That recipe is Marvel Meal, and if you're feeding birds on a budget, it's hard to beat. The whole batch is peanut butter, vegetable shortening, cornmeal, and flour. Odds are you've got all four in the cupboard right now.

Chickadees, titmice, and wrens come for the soft dough – and so do bluebirds, which don't always bother with a seed feeder. It's cheap, it keeps in the freezer, and kids can help mix it. And if you love helping birds in your backyard, then enter our competition to win a Birdfy smart feeder.

Its exact origin is hard to pin down, but bluebird fans have been passing the recipe around for years, and Penn State Extension still shares it today. There's nothing to cook and no beef fat to render, which some suet recipes call for. You also won't find a ring of spilled seed under the feeder the way you do with a seed mix.

Insect eaters get the most out of it. Bluebirds rarely eat seeds, and woodpeckers, nuthatches, and wrens lean on insects for much of the year. Come winter, bugs get hard to find. A rich, fatty food fills that gap with the calories birds need to stay warm through long nights, at a time when natural food can be scarce.

Beat the peanut butter and shortening together in a big bowl until it's smooth. Then work in the cornmeal and flour a cup or so at a time, and stir the seeds in last. You're after a soft dough that holds its shape when you squeeze a lump of it. If kids are helping, check for peanut allergies before anyone digs in.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Marvel Meal doesn't need to go in the fridge first. Soft is good, since that's what lets you press it into a feeder. If you'd rather have firm blocks for a suet feeder, spread the dough in a pan lined with wax paper, freeze it, and cut it into pieces.

Log feeders, like this Pennington red cedar suet feeder from Walmart, are the old standby. Press the dough into the drilled holes. You can also just smear some on rough bark or a pinecone, or fill half a coconut shell.

Place frozen blocks of Marvel Meal in a basic suet cage, like this Kingsyard all-metal double suet bird feeder with perch. The cage keeps squirrels and bigger birds from making off with the whole chunk. But never use a mesh onion bag – birds can get their feet tangled and stuck.

For bluebirds, roll the dough into small balls and set them in an open dish with some cover over it. Audubon's Woodlink dome-top seed and bluebird feeder, available at Home Depot, has a roof right above the dish. Wet weather turns the dough to mush, and a clear plastic squirrel baffle hung over a hanging feeder helps keep the rain off. Don't put out more than the birds will clean up in a day or two.

Penn State lists chickadees, titmice, wrens, and bluebirds as fans. Woodpeckers, nuthatches, blue jays, and even cardinals stop by too, though European starlings can turn into pests.

Bluebirds are the hard ones. They don't go to feeders the way chickadees do, and a lot of them have to learn that a dish means food. Who shows up in your yard depends on what lives around you and how you set out the food. Try a couple of spots and give it a few days. Hang feeders near trees or shrubs so small birds have somewhere to dart, just not so close that a hawk can sit hidden in them.

Marvel Meal is a winter treat, not a year-round meal. Start putting it out when the nights get cold in late fall and natural food is getting scarce. Birds don't need a steady diet of rich food, and heat brings its own problems. When highs climb to about 65°F to 70°F (18–21°C), the fat goes soft and can go rancid – and greasy food can mat feathers and even get onto eggs in a nest. Once spring stays warm, take it down.

Leftover dough keeps in sealed bags in the fridge, and the extra can go in the freezer. Keep seed somewhere cool and dry as well. The Gamma2 Vittles Vault from Walmart holds up to 35 pounds (16kg). Toss anything that's moldy, wet, or smells rancid. About every two weeks, scrub feeders in a mix of 1 part bleach to 9 parts water, and do it more often when it's wet or the feeders are busy. Rinse them well and let them dry before you fill them again.

Fill a log with Marvel Meal on a frosty morning, and a chickadee will probably find it before your coffee gets cold. Keep the batches small and the feeders clean, and they'll stick around all winter.

A mower that's running perfectly now might not be so cooperative after months in storage. A little preparation can help prevent costly surprises.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Ah, the last lawn-cutting Saturday comes and goes, so it’s the happy end of mowing for the entire calendar year. All you want to do is push that lawn mower into the shed and close and lock the door. But you can’t, and you’ll regret it if you do. Come the following spring, you’ll pull out a mower that is sluggish, with stale fuel, clogged carburetors, and broken parts. It’s entirely possible that that lawn mower won’t start in spring at all.

You can’t just put that mower to bed for a long winter’s nap without first doing some lawn mower maintenance. It’s not as nice as tucking that mower away and drinking a cool beer, but it’s not all that difficult either. Once you learn how to winterize a lawn mower, you’ll find that it’s easier to jump in and do the work before you move your machine into winter storage.

I'm here to walk you through the steps to prepare your lawn mower for its winter rest. Just follow this practical step-by-step approach. It won't take long if you tackle it alongside your other garden winterizing chores.

It only takes a month for the gasoline in a gas-powered motor to start to break down. When it does, it leaves gummy deposits in the carburetor. This doesn’t do anything good for the mower. You can tackle this in either of two ways.

First, and some would argue best, is to add a lawn mower fuel stabilizer to the remaining fresh gasoline in the tank. Sta-Bil, available on Amazon, is a good choice, but Sea Foam and Ethanol Shield are other popular options. But check your mower manufacturer's recommendations, as some don't advise this step.

To use a fuel stabilizer, first check the product instructions for the correct amount to add based on the gasoline volume. Add the stabilizer to the tank, then top up with fresh gasoline, leaving a little room for expansion. Run the engine for around 5-10 minutes, or as directed on the product label, to allow the treated fuel to circulate through the fuel system. This helps prevent gasoline from deteriorating during winter storage, reducing the risk of deposits forming in the carburetor and causing starting problems in spring.

The second option to winterize a gas mower is to empty the tank so that there is no gasoline to break down. You can do this easily by running the mower until it is totally out of gas. You can also empty the tank by draining the tank and carburetor bowl manually.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Before you start, switch off the engine, let it cool completely, and disconnect the spark plug wire for safety. If you need to tip the mower to access the underside, tilt it with the air filter and carburetor facing upward, as tipping it the wrong way can allow oil or fuel to leak into the air filter or engine intake.

Next, clean the underside of the mower, scraping away grass clippings and dirt with a plastic scraper or stiff nylon brush. Leaving damp debris in place over winter can cause corrosion on steel mower decks.

Once the underside is clean and completely dry, apply a protective coating. Mo-Deck Non-Stick Mower Deck Spray helps prevent grass clippings and debris from sticking to the deck, making cleanup easier when mowing season returns. Follow the product instructions and allow it to dry before storing the mower.

Draining the oil is not fun, but it’s not that difficult either. First, check your mower's manual, as some newer engines only require oil top-ups rather than regular changes. If yours needs an oil change, run the mower for a few minutes to warm the oil, then switch off the engine, let it cool enough to work safely, and disconnect the spark plug wire before proceeding.

Drain the old, dirty oil into a suitable container, following your mower's instructions. A Briggs & Stratton oil extractor kit makes the job much less messy, allowing you to remove oil through the fill tube without tipping the mower.

Does your mower have an oil filter? If so, change it now, using a replacement designed for your engine. Then refill with the correct amount of fresh motor oil. This will depend on your model, but common options include SAE 30 and synthetic 5W-30. Check the oil level with the dipstick to avoid overfilling, and take the used oil to a recycling facility.

Your lawn mower blade needs to be sharp and free of cracks. With the engine off and the spark plug wire disconnected, follow your mower's instructions to safely access and remove the blade. Wear thick gloves and check carefully for nicks, cracks, bends, or dull edges.

You can sharpen a dull blade with a hand file, but it's easier to use a proper lawn mower blade sharpener, like this Sporgain lawn mower blade sharpener and balancer from Amazon. However, if your lawn mower blade is cracked or badly damaged, it's better to replace it.

If you sharpen the blade yourself, follow the manufacturer's recommended angle and make sure it's properly balanced before reinstalling it. An unbalanced blade can cause excessive vibration and damage the mower.

At the same time, inspect the spark plug for wear, corrosion, or heavy carbon buildup. Remove it using a spark plug socket (this Milwaukee set from Home Depot has three sizes), and if the plug is damaged, badly worn, or heavily coated, it's best to replace it with a new one recommended for your mower. Otherwise, gently clean away any light buildup with a soft brush before putting it back. Check your mower's manual for any specific instructions.

The great thing about winterizing a battery-operated mower is that you don’t have to worry about gasoline issues. On the other hand, you do have to worry about looking after the battery. This is also important if your gasoline-powered mower has an electric starter.

Proper winter storage is essential. If the battery is removable, take it out of the mower and store it in a cool, dry place indoors, away from freezing temperatures and extreme heat. Check your manufacturer's recommendations for the ideal storage temperature, as requirements vary between batteries.

For lithium-ion batteries, most manufacturers recommend storing them partially charged, rather than fully charged or empty. Check the charge periodically throughout winter and top it up if needed.

However, if your mower uses a lead-acid battery, you generally need to keep it fully charged during storage. A compatible battery maintainer can help prevent them from going flat. The Noco Genius1 Smart Battery Charger and Maintainer maintains the battery's charge throughout winter so it's ready to go when mowing season returns. Do make sure any charger or maintainer you use is suitable for your battery type.

Move your mower into a dry shed, garage, or other sheltered space where it will be protected from rain, snow, and ice. Ideally, keep it on a clean, dry surface, as sitting on damp ground over winter can cause rust and corrosion.

A breathable, water-resistant lawn mower cover, like this Himal Outdoors Push Lawn Mower Cover from Amazon, is a good idea because it helps keep dust, dirt, and moisture off the mower when it's not in use. Make sure the mower is completely cool and dry before covering it.

Avoid storing your mower near corrosive household chemicals, fertilizers, or pool chlorine, as their fumes or spills can damage metal components over time. If you're storing it in a garage or shed, leave enough space around the machine for ventilation and easy access.

#7824. My New Book Chapter on How to Curb Dangerous Emergency Powers

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Now avaialble on SSRN. It is coauthored with Josh Braver, and will be published in the forthcoming Cato Handbook on Executive Power.

My forthcoming chapter on "Emergency Powers" is now available on SSRN. It is coauthored with Josh Braver (University of Wisconsin), and will be published in the forthcoming Cato Handbook on Executive Power, edited by Molly Nixon. Braver is a leading expert on the law of domestic use of the military and a liberal/progressive. I am a a libertarian. If we can come to agreement on these issues, I hope others can, as well. Here is the abstract:

Emergency powers are special types of government authorities that are only supposed to be used under extraordinary circumstances, in order to address a crisis. But, over time, many have become institutionalized as near-blank checks that the executive can invoke at will. This situation imperils civil liberties and our constitutional system.

This chapter goes over the major US emergency powers, including the National Emergencies Act, the Insurrection Act, the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), and others, and offers proposals for curbing the dangers they create. Effective reform requires a combination of new legislation and strong, nondeferential judicial review.

I recently covered related issues in an article for Just Security, which goes over potential legislative reforms. In the Cato Handbook chapter, Braver and I cover both legislative reforms and how judicial review can be strengthened.

It's easy to recreate the look in your own garden with beautiful white roses – and November is the perfect time to plant.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If there's one thing Miley Cyrus knows how to do, it's make a statement. And her recent wedding to musician Maxx Morando has given us plenty of inspiration – particularly when it comes to the flowers.

The couple's romantic ceremony featured masses of beautiful white roses, with a breathtaking floral arch creating a dreamy backdrop for the celebrations. It's classic, understated and wonderfully romantic. And, honestly? We're already dreaming about recreating the look in our own backyards. The good news is that November is one of the best times to get started. Bare-root roses are coming into season, making this the perfect opportunity to plant your own romantic rose display – often for considerably less than you'd spend on established container-grown plants.

So, while Miley might have had a team of florists to bring her wedding vision to life, you can take a slightly more long-term approach. Plant now, give your roses time to establish over winter, and you could be enjoying your own beautiful floral display come spring and summer. After all, as Miley herself once reminded us, we can absolutely buy ourselves flowers. But growing them ourselves? Even better.

There's something wonderfully timeless about an all-white flower display. While colorful planting schemes certainly have their place, sticking to one color can create a much more elegant look – and white roses, as Miley Cyrus' wedding photos have proven, are particularly lovely for this.

The beauty of this look is that you don't need hundreds of individual plants to make an impact. A well-positioned rose bush, a climbing variety trained over an arch or trellis, or even a small collection of white roses along a garden path can create a n atmosphere that's just as romantic.

Better still? Well, there's no need to wait until spring to start planning your own rose garden, because November is actually the ideal time to get planting. Bare-root roses become available from late fall and are generally much more affordable than their container-grown counterparts, making them a brilliant option if you're hoping to plant several together.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

If you're looking for something that combines good looks with wildlife appeal, this shrub rose produces fragrant white blooms, followed by ornamental rose hips that provide additional seasonal interest.

For something a little closer to the full-bodied blooms seen at Miley's wedding, this floribunda variety produces gorgeous double white blooms, sometimes with the faintest blush of pink.

Of course, if it's the dramatic floral arch you're hoping to recreate, you'll want to consider a climbing rose. This pretty variety is ideal for training over arches, pergolas and trellises.

The good news? You don't need an elaborate wedding installation to achieve that same Miley Cyrus-inspired look; you just need a sturdy garden arch like this pergola from Outsunny, and pop it somewhere that gets plenty of sunlight. (Most roses need at least six hours of direct sunlight each day).

Next, plant a climbing rose on either side of your structure, allowing the canes to grow and training them horizontally and upwards as they develop. Be patient, though, as your rose arch won't become an overnight sensation, and it may take a couple of growing seasons to achieve the look you're craving.

And there you have it: a little celebrity-inspired garden magic without the celebrity price tag. Miley Cyrus' wedding might have lasted just one day, but with the right roses and a little patience, you can enjoy your own romantic floral display year after year. Talk about a love story worth growing, eh?

#7821. Why Evergreen Shrubs Have Black or Brown Leaves in December – and When You Should Act Fast if You Spot This Leaf Damage

If you see evergreen shrubs with dead leaf tips in late fall or early winter, it's a sure sign you need to protect plants from frost, freezing temperatures and cold winds.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The mild fall in many areas this year allowed many shrubs to delay dormancy and even put out fresh growth. Without the time to build cold resistance before winter weather arrives, evergreen foliage is left vulnerable to leaf damage.

Blackened or brown evergreen leaf tips don't necessarily mean your shrubs are dying, but they are cause for concern and a clear sign you need to prepare your garden for winter. Understanding what's caused the damage is important so you know what to do next to save your beloved evergreen shrubs. So, great work getting here to Garden ER where you'll find straightforward solutions to treat this season’s biggest planty problems. Come on in and let’s diagnose and treat your evergreen shrubs with black or brown leaf tips in late fall or early winter.

If your shrubs are experiencing damage related to our mild fall this year, you're likely to spot these symptoms:

If the damage is confined to a few leaf and needle tips, there's no need to worry: your shrub will recover, and it's a good idea to take steps to prevent further damage. If the damage is more significant, there's still a high chance of recovery but you should better protect plants from frost and have plenty of patience.

There are two primary and most likely causes of dark, dry tips on your evergreen shrubs. The distinction matters because the underlying cause determines how you help your shrub recover.

Your shrubs naturally harden off for winter, a process triggered by less daylight and gradually dropping temperatures. They slow their growth and undergo some internal processes that allow them to better withstand freezing winter temperatures. To get more specific, soluble sugars begin to accumulate in the cells of leaves and needles. These sugars make it harder for water in the cells to freeze and allow the plant to better regulate water movement. As the youngest leaves go through this process, they become woodier, more mature, and more resistant to freezing injuries.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

During a mild fall, as many of us have experienced this year, some evergreens might continue producing new, soft growth instead of entering the dormancy period. This disrupts the vital process of winter hardening-off, leaving cells with high water content and underdeveloped protection. So, when temperatures finally drop, the water in cells freezes more readily. These frozen cells then rupture. Affected leaves, needles, and tips die as a result of the damage and turn brown or black.

Some of the evergreens most susceptible to this type of damage include hebe, choisya, camellia, and photinia. Even plants that normally tolerate cold winters can be affected after an unusually warm fall.

Desiccation or wind scorch, also known as winter burn, is another potential cause of black or brown evergreen foliage, and this can occur regardless of an unseasonable fall. Evergreen shrubs lose moisture through their leaves, even as growth slows, and cold air, winter winds and bright sun increase this moisture loss. Once the ground – and the moisture held in the soil – freezes, the shrubs’ roots can't take up water to replace what's being lost. This moisture imbalance can cause leaf and needle tissue to dry out and turn brown or black, and damage often begins at foliage tips and margins.

Distinguishing leaf damage caused by winter desiccation from new foliage that's died in the first cold snap is easy: if wind scorch is the issue, damage will be on the windy side of the shrub. You’ll also see that the outer leaves and needles are most affected, with the inner foliage protected. The damage from wind scorch is typically gradual rather than suddenly appearing after a frost or freeze, too.

Evergreens with shallow roots like arborvitae, boxwood, rhododendron, yew, juniper and holly are particularly susceptible to winter desiccation. Any evergreen can be damaged this way, however, depending on moisture in the soil, wind levels and how protected the shrub is.

First – and most importantly – of all, don’t rush to snip off those black tips. You can’t recover that dead tissue, and cutting it off now can cause more damage. If your shrubs are victims of the poor hardening-off that resulted from a mild fall, trimming could trigger more vulnerable growth, and also expose currently sheltered foliage to further harm. Similarly, the damage on a wind-scorched shrub will protect the foliage beneath.

The next step depends on the cause of the leaf damage.

Now you know your shrub isn’t ready for the cold, protect it from the rest of the winter weather to come. A zip-up plant jacket is an easy way to winterize shrubs that only need protecting ahead of a predicted cold snap rather than being wrapped up all winter. Another option is to wrap plants up in burlap – rolls of hessian are available from Walmart – or horticultural fleece such as this from Amazon, unwrapping plants after the cold weather has passed.

When covering shrubs, be sure to do so loosely and use stakes inserted in the soil to hold fabric away from leaves. If your shrub is growing in a container, then wrapping the pot in bubble wrap and burlap protects roots during a prolonged freeze, too. Choose the level of protection based on your zone and how badly damaged your evergreen shrub is.

If those dead leaf tips are caused by a wind and moisture imbalance, first check the moisture in the soil around the plants. If you're using a moisture meter, make sure it's one with a long probe like this moisture meter on Amazon so you get a reading where it matters. If the soil is dry and the ground isn’t frozen, give the root zone a good soak.

Next, apply a layer of mulch made from natural materials like Back to the Roots Organic Mulch, available from Amazon, around the base of each shrub. This will help conserve moisture and insulate the soil. Just be sure to keep the mulch a few inches away from the stems to prevent moisture accumulating there and causing rot or fungal disease.

Now you need to protect your shrub from further damage from wind scorch. You could pop a frost jacket on your shrub whenever high winds are forecast, or use burlap to create a windbreak. You don’t necessarily need to cover the whole shrub; just provide a barrier from the prevailing winds. Keep checking shrubs throughout the winter, adding windbreaks and watering when the soil thaws as needed.

These steps will help prevent more damage, but they won’t reverse the damage that has already occurred. Now, you’re probably wondering when you can remove those unsightly dead leaf tips – and you're going to have to be patient. It’s important not to prune off dead leaves or branches now as this can trigger new growth, introduce damage or disease at the cut areas, and leave interior foliage vulnerable.

Wait to prune until spring when there is no more risk of a severe frost, then use clean, sharp shears to remove dead tips. If larger areas have browned or blackened, cut these stems back to the first healthy, live bud. You can check if a branch might regrow by scraping back the outer layer with your fingernail. If it’s brown underneath, it’s dead and should be removed. If you see green, it could still sprout new growth.

Keep your pruning light in spring. Trim back the damaged parts and then let healthy branches and leaves grow back in before you do any heavier pruning or shaping.

The damage for this year is done and gone, but you can learn from the incident to save your evergreen shrubs from harm next year:

Dead leaf tips on evergreen shrubs are usually a cosmetic issue, not a death sentence for your favorite plants. Follow these guidelines and your shrubs should recover, ready to shine again next year.

#7820. Autumn in a Montana Garden

Hi GPOD! Longtime contributor Kielian is back today with another beautiful look at her garden in Hamilton, Montana. We’ve followed this garden through the seasons for years, and GPOD readers may even remember Kielian’s first autumn tour from more than a decade ago. Today she’s sharing what fall looks like on the ranch nearly 17 years into the garden’s evolution.

In the Bitterroot Valley of Montana, fall imparts her special light and changing colors to the ranch. The gardens are closing in on 17 years of beauty and, interestingly, have decided which design they like the most… on their own.

My detailed blueprints and drawings of plantings have been changed by Mother Nature, who knows so much more than I do about proper placement. Birds deposit valuable seeds in areas I would never have approved of, and the failure of certain plants to survive makes room for those that forge ahead with gusto. Ahh, autumn, how delightful are your colors and resilience.

Late October in Montana: The ‘Pee Wee’ oakleaf hydrangeas (Hydrangea quercifolia ‘Pee Wee’, Zones 5–9) are showing off, and the ornamental pear tree was not going to be outdone.

The front garden early in the morning: Shadows enhance the color changes.

The back deck was sprinkled with maple-tree graffiti. The linden tree boasted brilliant yellow, and a gorgeous crabapple by the pump house screamed for attention with bright red leaves.

A smokebush (Cotinus coggygria, Zones 4–8) and aspen tree drip with early morning rain.

A golden sunset scattered early October rays on quaking aspens (Populus tremuloides, Zones 1–6), enhanced by the Bitterroot Mountains as a backdrop.

Tessa came running along the path through early November changing leaves.

An ornamental pear tree with fading black-eyed Susans in front. Winter is on her way.

Thanks for sharing another season in your garden with us, Kielian! After seeing this garden in spring, summer, fall, and even covered in snow over the years, it’s hard to pick a favorite season. But that golden sunset over the pond with the Bitterroot Mountains in the distance certainly makes a strong case for fall!

#7819. Virginia Needn't Help with Federal Immigration Enforcement, But Can't Interfere With It

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From today's decision in U.S. v. Virginia, by Judge Toby Heytens, joined by Judge DeAndrea Gist Benjamin:

[W]e vacate a preliminary injunction preventing the Commonwealth of Virginia from rendering unenforceable existing agreements between the Federal Government and the Commonwealth's state or local agencies "to perform [the] function[s] of a federal immigration officer" unless certain conditions are met. The Federal Government may not "command" the Commonwealth's "officers, or those of [its] political subdivisions" (Printz v. U.S. (1997)) to assist with federal immigration enforcement efforts, and the Commonwealth's supreme lawmaking body has imposed new limits on when its agents may agree to do so. That choice does not violate the intergovernmental immunity doctrine because it neither requires the Federal Government to do anything nor limits any private party's ability to contract with the Federal Government.

It also does not violate the Federal Constitution's Contracts Clause for two separate reasons: (1) because the existing agreements all expressly permit the non-federal party to unilaterally terminate without cause; and (2) even if they did not, the Commonwealth would have constitutionally valid justifications for imposing new terms for future cooperation in any event….

[But] we affirm a preliminary injunction forbidding enforcement of a new state law that regulates when federal employees may wear facial coverings and must display visible identification while performing their federal duties…. [J]ust as Congress may not "issue orders directly to the States," States may not issue orders directly to the Federal Government. We thus conclude the law at issue violates the intergovernmental immunity doctrine….

Our holding is limited. We reiterate that "an employee of the United States does not secure a general immunity from state law while acting in the course of his employment," and we make no effort to provide a full list of situations in which federal officers may or may not be prosecuted for violating state law.

We also emphasize that neither the Federal Government's broad authority in immigration matters, nor "the history and context for the enactment of" the Mask/Identity Law play any role in our analysis. Whether the Mask/Identity Law directly regulates the Federal Government does not depend on what motivated the Commonwealth's decision to enact the law or whether its various provisions (or the practices that prompted them) represent wise policy.

Finally, we do not address whether other legal requirements—including the Fourth Amendment—limit the permissible use of masked and otherwise-unidentified law enforcement officers….

Judge Robert King agreed with the majority as to the likely validity of Virginia's refusal to assist with immigration enforcement, but dissented as to the mask/identity statute. For the full (long) opinions, see here.

NEXT: My New Book Chapter on How to Curb Dangerous Emergency Powers

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast.

Would a mini greenhouse or a cold frame be best for your garden needs this winter? Here's everything you need to know to decide…

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When the forecast drops below freezing for the first time in late fall, half the neighborhood rushes out to tuck bedsheets over their mums – unless they have a greenhouse, that is. But while most folk don't have the space or the budget for a full-size glasshouse, a mini greenhouse or cold frame is the affordable option to get plants through winter unscathed. But which is best when it comes to protecting plants from winter weather?

A mini greenhouse is a tall but narrow enclosure with wire-mesh shelves zipped inside a clear plastic cover. A cold frame is a low, bottomless box with a see-through lid that sits right on the dirt. Both catch sun all day, but they handle the night very differently, making the best one for you dependant on what you grow. And a Georgia winter is a very different beast from a Minnesota one, which affects how you winterize your garden in late fall.

Here's everything you need to know to make the right decision to protect your plants from frost and snow this winter.

Most mini greenhouses are made from a light steel frame with two to four tiers of wire-mesh shelves. This is covered with a PVC or polyethylene cover that zips up the front, or some designs have rigid polycarbonate panels, which is why they're often referred to as 'plastic greenhouses'. To vent, you unzip and roll up the door.

Mini greenhouses are cheap and give you a lot of growing space for a small footprint, but the plastic cover can wear out and be hard to replace, and not all products stand up to winter winds unless they're positioned in a sheltered spot. If you only use a mini greenhouse in winter, it's easy to pack up and store away for summer, or if you can remove the shelves then they're useful for growing tomatoes.

Cold frames are typically made from wood, aluminum or brick with a hinged glass or polycarbonate lid that can be propped open on warm days. Only holding one layer of pots, a cold frame and will only fit fairly low-growing plants. They generally cost more, unless you put your DIY skills to the test and build your own cold frame, but a sturdy design with a rigid lid lasts for years. A cold frame doesn't buy you any extra growing room, however.

Plants will usually come through a harsh 20°F (-7°C) night better in a cold frame than a mini greenhouse. Because the frame has an open base and sits directly on the ground, it benefits more from the heat of the sun. Soil soaks up the solar heat all day, which is why it's a good idea to prop the lid open a few inches on sunny days if temperatures rise above 40°F (4°C). But close the lid by late afternoon and the interior stays warm as the soil gives the heat back overnight, and the frame's solid sides slow the loss. For extra warmth, it's an easy task to bank straw or soil against the walls. too.

So, vegetables such as lettuce, spinach, kale and other winter greens will keep growing slowly under a cold frame lid into early winter. Low perennials and young transplants often do well too, and so do plants that rot when winter rain sits on their crowns.

Space is where a mini greenhouse wins over a cold frame. With several tiers of shelves, you can stack seedling trays, rooted cuttings and pots of hardy herbs in a space about the size of a doormat. However, a mini greenhouse sitting on paving has no soil to draw from, so it doesn't stay as warm overnight. While the interior still heats up in the day (so needs venting), thin plastic sides allow the warmth to quickly escape, so it doesn't take long for the air inside to drop to the same temperature as the air outside. A tall mini greenhouse catches every gust of wind, too, and cold air finds any gaps around zippers and seams.

If you have a sheltered sunny wall to stand a mini greenhouse against, however, that structure will absorb the sun's heat during the day and give it back through the night, helping to stabilize temperatures. Still, don't trust thin plastic in a hard freeze – but a mini greenhouse does a great job at keeping wind and rain off hardy container plants.

A mini greenhouse gives you extra growing space on a balcony or in a small urban garden, too.

When buying a cold frame, it's good to know that wood insulates better than metal if you live in a harsh climate. It's heavier, though, so if you want to be able to move your cold frame, then an aluminum frame also has the advantage it won't rot. Either way, look for a sturdy frame that doesn't wobble and a lid that props open at more than one height. Automatic venting is a useful upgrade if you're not at home during the day, as a temperature-activated hinge lifts the lid as the inside warms up.

Cedar wood frame, 3.5mm polycarbonate insulation and fully opening lid with venting positions.

Aluminum frame, 4mm polycarbonate panels and a collapsible design for easy summer storage.

Cedar and powder-coated steel, double-wall polycarbonate lid and temperature-activated automatic lid opening.

When buying a mini greenhouse, there's a balance to be had between budget and cover quality. A mini greenhouse with polycarbonate panels is more expensive but holds heat far better than a floppy plastic cover. If you opt for a cheaper flexible cover then look for one made of PE (polyethylene), preferably reinforced PE, rather than PVC.

PE stays flexible in freezing temperature and copes with long-term UV exposure well. PE that's reinforced with mesh also means any rips are easily fixed, and still lets in around 85% of sunlight. PVC (polyvinyl chloride) is usually clearer so lets more light through, but tends to split and yellow over time.

Look for a stiff, robust frame because a wobbly one means the cover flaps until the seams gape. It's vital that you can anchor the mini greenhouse down, too, and that the method used is suitable for the ground you plant to stand it on. Most designs will have base flaps that you can weigh down with bricks or stones, while some offer additional anchoring with ground stakes – useful if your garden is at all exposed.

Double-layer roof design for ventilation, UV-resistant PE cover and zip-up door. Measures 50" H x 27.6" W x 19.7" D.

Reinforced PE cover, mesh racks and 4 ropes and ground stakes. Measures 76.8" H x 57.9" W x 30.3" D.

4mm polycarbonate panels, roof vent, sliding door and rain gutter. Measures 71.65" H x 75.98" W x 27.16" D.

It's a simple task to upgrade a cold frame or mini greenhouse when winterizing your garden, and the cheap fixes go a long way. You could save bubble wrap to repurpose in the garden, clipping a layer inside the cover for an extra layer of trapped air. Always pick big bubbles since they generally insulate better, like this 24-inch-wide roll of large-bubble clear wrap from Amazon. Bubble wrap does cut some light, however, and packing-grade wrap breaks down in the sun faster than horticultural film.

On a bitter night, spreading frost cloth like this from Amazon over the plants inside also helps to insulate them, and it's easily pulled off in the morning.

A tall mini greenhouse can tip in strong wind, and even if anchoring stakes are included, they're usually flimsy. A shed anchor kit like this from Amazon with 18-inch ground screws and steel cable will do a much better job of holding your mini greenhouse down through winter weather.

If you mostly grow winter greens and low perennials, buy the cold frame since the open soil base and solid sides will give plants steadier nights. If you need plenty of space for seedlings, cuttings or taller pots, go with a mini greenhouse and expect bigger temperature swings.

Whichever you pick, park it in a sunny spot out of the wind, and hang a cheap digital max/min thermometer like this from Amazon in there so you know just what degree of winter protection your plants are getting. Neither a cold frame nor a mini greenhouse will protect frost-tender plants in severe cold weather without extra insulation or a safe heat source, so bring them inside before a hard freeze. And if you do add heat, do it carefully – a soil-heating cable on a GFCI outlet turns a cold frame into a hotbed, but keep heaters away from plastic and never run a fuel-burning heater in a small closed structure.

#7817. Small Moments at Season’s End

Hey, garden gang! Longtime contributor Susan Warde is back today with a closer look at her garden in St. Paul, Minnesota. We’ve seen what the end of the season looks like in Susan’s garden before, but today she’s focusing on the smaller details that are easy to overlook this time of year.

I understand the reasons for not cutting down perennials and for letting leaves lie untouched over the winter, but it takes me about 10 weeks to clean up. I have a large garden, family commitments, unpredictable weather, and a limited number of yard-waste bags that our pickup service will take at one time. Ten weeks in the spring would put me into mid-June before I could get the weeds and overwintered mess under control.

So I’ve been cleaning up, and the garden has been looking pretty bare recently, positively grim on overcast days. But during the process I was struck by small vignettes of beauty that stood out in an otherwise desolate landscape.

The underside of some Korean maple leaves (Acer pseudosieboldianum, Zones 4–8)

A ‘Northern Hi-Lights’ azalea (Rhododendron ‘Northern Hi-Lights’, Zones 4–7) with bright fall color… and buds that promise spring

The seed head of ‘Guernsey Flute’ clematis (Clematis ‘Guernsey Flute’, Zones 4–9) that had a second late flowering

One last blossom on a ‘Max Frei’ bloody cranesbill (Geranium sanguineum ‘Max Frei’, Zones 3–8)

Raindrops on columbine (Aquilegia cvs., Zones 3–8) leaves

The yellowed leaves of a bulblet fern (Cystopteris bulbifera, Zones 3–8) that I’d overlooked during the cutting-down process

A bee enjoys the very last plant in bloom, black cohosh (Actaea racemosa, Zones 3–8).

Evergreen Christmas fern (Polystichum acrostichoides, Zones 3–8) and moss

I had never before looked closely at the bark of a blue beech (Carpinus caroliniana, Zones 3–9), which from a distance just looks taupe.

Five minutes before taking the photo, I’d cleaned out this birdbath—the one I leave available in winter, and then only on above-freezing days. The leaves are from a ‘North Wind’ maple (Acer × pseudosieboldianum ‘IslNW’, Zones 4–7).

Thanks for sharing these small moments from your garden, Susan! There are so many things to love about a garden, but I often find that the small details people tend to gloss over are even more reason to celebrate. There’s so much happening at once! You just have to look closely to see it. (:

#7816. Fourth Circuit Upholds Virginia's Law Terminating Agreements to Help With Immigration Enforcement - but Strikes Down anti-Mask Law

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

The ruling on Section 287(g) agreements overturns an earlier district court decision.

In September, I wrote about the the federal district court decision striking down Virginia's new law terminating Section 287(g) agreements, under which various state and local law enforcement agencies agree to help with federal immigration enforcement. Today, in United States v. Virginia, the US Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit reversed that decision. But, at the same time, in a 2-1 ruling, they struck down Virginia's law barring law enforcement officers (including federal ones) from wearing masks except in relatively narrowly specified circumstances. Here is an excerpt from the court's opinion (written by Judge Heytens) on the 287(g) issue:

We vacate the preliminary injunction that bars enforcing the 287(g) Law with respect to existing agreements. The district court concluded the Federal Government was likely to succeed on the merits because rendering such agreements unenforceable violate both the intergovernmental immunity doctrine and the Contracts Clause. We disagree. The intergovernmental immunity doctrine does not apply because the 287(g) Law neither directly regulates the Federal Government nor prevents private parties from contracting with it…. The 287(g) Law also does not violate the Contracts Clause for two separate reasons: (1) because the existing agreements expressly permit unilateral termination by the non-federal party; and (2) even if they did not, the Commonwealth would have constitutionally valid justifications for requiring state and local officials to terminate or renegotiate any such agreements.

Later in the opinion Judge Heytens expands on why Section 287(g) termination does not violate the Contracts Clause:

We conclude the Federal Government cannot satisfy that test for two different, yet complementary, reasons. First, all the agreements covered by the district court's injunction expressly permit the Commonwealth's agents to unilaterally terminate without cause, which means the 287(g) Law does not "substantially impair" (Sveen, 584 U.S. at 819) a contractual relationship at Step 1. Second, even if the agreements did not so provide, neither the Commonwealth's agencies nor those of its localities may contract away "an essential attribute of [the Commonwealth's] sovereignty." United States Tr. Co. of N.Y. v. New Jersey, 431 U.S. 1, 23 (1977). Here, that attribute is the Commonwealth's power to decide whether and on what terms to assist with the ongoing enforcement of federal law.

I largely agree. In my post on the district court decision, I offered some additional reasons why terminating these agreements doesn't violate the Contracts Clause.

The anti-mask law presents more difficult issues because - as the majority emphasizes - it directly regulates federal law enforcement officials. On the other hand, the law imposes the same constraints on state and local officers, as well, and therefore doesn't discriminate against them. On balance, I agree with Judge Robert Bruce King's dissent:

At bottom, a single ICE officer should never be able to override a duly enacted statute of the Commonwealth of Virginia in the absence of some federal law, regulation, or other valid supporting authority. Consider what purportedly conflicts with the Mask/Identity Statute. A federal statute? None. A treaty of the United States? None. A federal regulation or executive order? None. A written policy located anywhere within ICE or the Department of Homeland Security? None has been identified. What we have today is a single sentence in a Declaration asserting that individual ICE officers possess the discretion and ability to conceal their identities when they alone deem it appropriate. No supervision is at all necessary or required and the agency itself has no involvement in the ICE officer's daily decisions on whether to wear a mask. I cannot and will not accept the proposition that individualized discretion, untethered to any identifiable source of federal law, enjoys constitutional supremacy over a duly enacted statute of the Commonwealth.

As the majority recognizes, federal law enforcement officers are not generally exempt from state law while on the job. For example, they must obey state traffic laws when driving their vehicles. A valid federal law could override a conflicting state law. But here, there is no such overriding federal law, or even a regulation (though I'm not convinced the latter alone would be enough). Just the preferences of ICE agents. Those preferences are not enough to secure an exemption from state law.  Federal law (when constitutionally valid) is supreme over state law. The preferences of individual federal officials or agencies are not.

NEXT: Virginia Needn't Help with Federal Immigration Enforcement, But Can't Interfere With It

Ilya Somin is Visiting Professor of Law at the University of Virginia, Professor of Law at George Mason University, Simon Chair in Constitutional Studies at the Cato Institute, and author of Free to Move: Foot Voting, Migration, and Political Freedom, Democracy and Political Ignorance: Why Smaller Government is Smarter, and The Grasping Hand: Kelo v. City of New London and the Limits of Eminent Domain.

#7815. From the GPOD Archives: Colorful Carnivores

Hi GPOD! We’re digging into the archives today for a garden that looks a little otherworldly. Jeff Calton gardens in Northeast Tennessee (Zone 6b/7a), where he grows an incredible collection of pitcher plants (Sarracenia cvs., Zones 5–9). Even better is how he grows them: Jeff sinks containers with minimal drainage into his regular garden beds, creating the boggy conditions these carnivorous plants need while allowing completely different plants to grow right alongside them. Such a clever way to work around varying growing conditions!

White-topped pitcher plant (Sarracenia leucophylla, Zones 5–8) has leaves that are more colorful than most flowers.

Yellow pitcher plant (Sarracenia flava, Zones 6–9) isn’t as brightly colored as some species, but it has a grace and elegance all its own.

‘Scarlet Belle’ pitcher plant (Sarracenia × ‘Scarlet Belle’, Zones 5–10) glows in front of a mixed planting including ‘Golden Duchess’ eastern hemlock (Tsuga canadensis ‘Golden Duchess’, Zones 3–7).

Close-up of the graceful pitchers of a yellow pitcher plant ready to lure in an insect meal

The pitcher plants in the back are growing in a sunken bathtub, giving them the wet soil they need, while the sedum and sedges in front have the better-drained conditions they require.

When I came across this post in the archives, I knew I had to share it again with you all! These pitcher plants are amazing, and for whatever reason, photo 2 makes me feel like I’m looking into a fish tank. I would love to see what Jeff’s garden looks like today. Jeff, if you’re still reading GPOD, send us an update! What a fantastic garden.
